summary: Describes OAKLEY, a protocol in which two authenticated parties agree on shared secret keying material using the Diffie-Hellman key exchange as its basic mechanism. It influenced the design of IKE. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends can mix paint colors in public so that both end up with a secret color nobody else can work out. OAKLEY uses that idea to share a secret.

questions: what is the oakley key determination protocol
how does oakley relate to isakmp and ike
subtitle: A key exchange protocol built on Diffie-Hellman that lets two authenticated parties pick secret keys, with optional extras for privacy and forward secrecy.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic protection of Internet traffic needs a scalable, secure way for two parties to agree on secret keys and to be sure who they are talking to.
tldr.mechanism: OAKLEY uses a Diffie-Hellman exchange, authenticated by signatures, public key encryption or an existing shared key, plus anti-clogging cookies, negotiable algorithms and selectable groups.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational. It is described as compatible with ISAKMP, and the exact mapping of OAKLEY fields to ISAKMP payloads was left to a separate Resolution document.

facts.label: Minimum nonce size
facts.value: At least 90 bits if no group is given

today: RFC 2412 is Informational, and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The text itself says that its ISAKMP field mapping was still in progress and that the transforms and the Resolution document would be defined separately.

sections.title: Why OAKLEY Exists
sections.content:
Key establishment is the heart of data protection that relies on cryptography, so the Internet needs a scalable and secure key distribution mechanism. RFC 2412 describes OAKLEY, a protocol by which two authenticated parties agree on secure and secret keying material. Its basic mechanism is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which lets two parties agree on a shared value without encrypting it.

OAKLEY is related to the STS protocol, which authenticates the Diffie-Hellman values. It adds a weak address check with cookies to resist denial of service, lets the parties negotiate the encryption, hash and authentication algorithms, and lets them choose or define their own Diffie-Hellman groups. It supports perfect forward secrecy, key updates and incorporating keys distributed out of band.

The generated keys might protect data with a long privacy lifetime, 20 years or more, so the algorithms must be chosen with that in mind.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks only help if two people can agree on a secret key without anyone listening in. OAKLEY is a careful way to agree on one.

sections.title: Cookies, Key Names and Notation
sections.content:
Each side contributes a 64-bit pseudo-random cookie at the start. The cookies work as a weak proof that the sender can see replies sent to its address, and the cookie exchange can finish before the costly large-integer math begins. The pair of cookies also becomes the KEYID, the reusable name of the keying material. The keying material itself, sKEYID, is never transmitted.

Messages are written as arrows between the Initiator and the Responder, with fields such as CKY-I, CKY-R, the message type OK_KEYX, a group name GRP, the half-keys g^x and g^y, nonces Ni and Nr, and the lists of encryption, hash and authentication choices, EHAO (offered) and EHAS (selected). Unused fields are null values.

OAKLEY is designed to be a compatible component of ISAKMP, which runs over UDP, and needs only that the stack can supply the remote Internet address. The host must have a good random number generator (see RFC 1750).
sections.plainLanguage: Each side shows a secret handshake token called a cookie. Matching tokens prove they can hear each other, and together the two tokens become the name of the secret they build.

sections.title: How an Exchange Runs
sections.content:
A key exchange has three parts: a cookie exchange (optionally stateless), the Diffie-Hellman half-key exchange, and authentication. Features such as stateless cookies, perfect forward secrecy, identity secrecy and signatures are optional, and any combination can be used. With no stateless cookies and no identity secrecy, the exchange can finish in three messages; more features need more round trips.

In the aggressive example the Initiator sends everything at once: cookie, group, g^x, algorithm offers, identities, a nonce and a digital signature. The Responder answers with its own half-key and signature, and the Initiator confirms. The result is sKEYID = prf(Ni | Nr, g^xy | CKY-I | CKY-R). The Responder may accept all, part or none of the offer, working left to right, and fields it does not accept come back as null.

In the conservative example the parties start with a bare cookie request, delay creating state and use perfect forward secrecy to hide identities. If both cookies are zero the message is a request for a cookie. The Initiator is responsible for retransmitting if the exchange does not finish in time.
sections.plainLanguage: You can do the whole handshake in one big rushed go, or slowly, one careful step at a time, hiding your names until you are sure. The fast way takes fewer turns; the careful way keeps more secret.

sections.title: Identity and Authentication
sections.content:
The Initiator offers two identities: its own claimed identity and the requested identity of the Responder. If neither is given, they are taken from the source and destination addresses in the IP header. The Responder can reply with a different identity, which the Initiator may accept by continuing or refuse by stopping.

Authentication can use digital signatures, public key encryption or an out-of-band symmetric key. The methods the RFC lists are:

  • Pre-shared keys: support is REQUIRED.
  • DNS public keys: implementations must support DNS KEY and SIG records for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and fully qualified domain names, though no particular algorithm is required.
  • RSA public keys without a certification authority (PGP style), and RSA or DSS keys with certificates: both OPTIONAL.

Support for accessing and revoking public key certificates through secure DNS is MANDATORY. The authentication must validate the g^x and g^y values and must not depend circularly on them, so that a man-in-the-middle can reveal identities at worst but cannot make authentication succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sharing a secret you check ID. You can compare a secret password you already share, look someone up in a phone book you trust, or check a signed card.

sections.title: Private Groups, Quick Mode and External Keys
sections.content:
OAKLEY can do more than a single Diffie-Hellman exchange. Parties can build a private group over an already authenticated key, so an attacker would face many different groups instead of one or two well-known ones. The new group identifier is built from truncated nonces, and the group description is protected by the earlier key.

Quick mode derives a new key from an existing authenticated key using only hashing: the new KEYID is Ni | Nr and the new key is prf(sKEYID, Ni | Nr). An external key distributed by other means can be carried under an existing OAKLEY key by XOR with a derived value, and the RFC says this needs no encryption. Manually distributed keys can also be used if they carry the usual state of identities and algorithm choices.

The protecting key must be at least as strong as the external key it distributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Once two friends share a secret, they can use it to invent new secrets quickly, or even to make up a new secret code book that outsiders have never seen.

sections.title: Group Choices and Security Notes
sections.content:
Three kinds of Diffie-Hellman group can be described: modular exponentiation (MODP) and two kinds of elliptic curve groups (EC2N and ECP). Appendix E lists well-known group identifiers, and values 2^31 and higher are for private groups. Groups 1 and 2 are Sophie Germain prime groups built from the binary expansion of pi so nobody can suspect they were secretly chosen to be weak.

For roughly 90 bits of strength the RFC suggests a modulus of at least 1400 bits and a largest prime factor of at least 180 bits, with exponents of at least 180 bits. It also warns that values 1 and p-1 must not be accepted as exponentials. Implementations should defend against timing attacks that recover the exponent, for example with a random blinding factor, which the RFC says is needed only if the exponent is used more than 100 times.

The Security Considerations section is a single remark: the document is about security, so security considerations permeate it. Error messages are informational only and the protocol's correctness does not depend on them.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger numbers make the puzzle harder to crack, so the RFC says how big to make them. It also says to be careful not to leak hints about your secret by how long the math takes.
